title: Ionic bonding
learningObjective: Understand how ions are formed by electron loss or gain; Know the charges of these ions: metals in Groups 1, 2 and 3; non-metals in Groups 5, 6 and 7; Ag⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Pb²⁺, Zn²⁺; hydrogen (H⁺), hydroxide (OH⁻), ammonium (NH₄⁺), carbonate (CO₃²⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻), sulfate (SO₄²⁻); Write formulae for compounds formed between the ions listed above; Draw dot-and-cross diagrams to show the formation of ionic compounds by electron transfer, limited to combinations of elements from Groups 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 (only outer electrons need be shown); Understand ionic bonding in terms of electrostatic attractions; Understand why compounds with giant ionic lattices have high melting and boiling points; Know that ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid, but do conduct electricity when molten and in aqueous solution

sections.title: Ionic bonding — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Chapter 7 takes the compound idea from Chapter 2 and finally explains what
"chemically combined" means for the most common family of compounds on the
course. The book opens with the everyday proof: sodium is a dangerously
reactive metal stored under oil, chlorine is a poisonous reactive gas — but
the compound they form, sodium chloride, is safe to eat in small quantities.
The properties of a compound are nothing like the properties of its elements,
and this chapter explains why: in ionic compounds the atoms have **transferred
electrons** and become charged ions.

All of the objectives of record for this lesson are **core** specification
statements — examined in **both Paper 1 (1C) and Paper 2 (2C)**, and shared
with Science Double Award:

- how **ions are formed by electron loss or gain** (spec 1.37);
- the **charges** on ions of Group 1/2/3 metals, Group 5/6/7 non-metals, and
  the named ions Ag⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Pb²⁺, Zn²⁺, H⁺, OH⁻, NH₄⁺, CO₃²⁻,
  NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ (spec 1.38);
- **writing formulae** for compounds between those ions (spec 1.39);
- **dot-and-cross diagrams** for electron transfer, outer electrons only
  (spec 1.40);
- ionic bonding as **electrostatic attraction** (spec 1.41);
- why **giant ionic lattices** have high melting and boiling points (spec 1.42);
- **conductivity**: no conduction when solid, conduction when molten or in
  aqueous solution (spec 1.43).

The chapter runs pp. 75–83 in three movements: forming ions and showing the
transfer with dot-and-cross diagrams (pp. 75–78), then the formula shortcut —
equal pluses and minuses, with the learn-list of ion charges (pp. 78–81), then
the giant-lattice structure and the properties that follow from it (pp. 81–83).
The book's end-of-chapter questions (p. 83) stay outside this Lesson — open the
student book PDF for those.

:::prior-knowledge
The book says the chapter builds straight on work you have already done, and
the three load-bearing pieces are: the **definition of a compound** from
Chapter 2 (u1:c02 — two or more elements chemically combined); **electronic
configurations** from Chapter 3 (u1:c03) — you need [2, 8, 1] for sodium and
[2, 8, 7] for chlorine without hesitation; and **groups of the Periodic Table**
from Chapter 4 (u1:c04) — the group number tells you how many outer-shell
electrons an atom has, which is what decides the ion charge. If writing [2, 8,
8, 2] for calcium feels slow, revisit u1:c03/c04 first.
:::

:::exam-hint
Every objective in this chapter is core — it can be asked in Paper 1 or Paper
2, by every candidate including Double Award. Ion charges and formulae
(1.38/1.39) are the recall backbone of dozens of later questions: equations,
titrations, salt preparations and electrolysis all assume you can write
Na₂O or Fe₂(SO₄)₃ without hesitating. Treat the Table-7.2 learn-list in
section 6 as non-negotiable memory work — it pays out across the whole
qualification, not just this chapter.
:::

:::misconception
"This is a brand-new topic, so it starts from scratch." It doesn't — it *uses*
Chapter 3 and 4 rather than replacing them. Every statement in this chapter is
the electronic-configuration idea pointed at a new job: the group number
(Chapter 4) predicts the charge; the outer shell (Chapter 3) is the only part
drawn in a dot-and-cross diagram. Learners who file ionic bonding as a separate
subject memorise; learners who see it as configurations-in-action derive.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.37–1.43 items — the seven-objective
map, the both-papers route badge, and the compounds-versus-elements property
contrast that opens the chapter. Book p. 83 questions 1–2 → page jump only
(licensing law).
:::

sections.title: Forming ions — sodium chloride
sections.markdown:
Sodium chloride is the book's flagship example: an **[[ion]]ic** compound
formed when a metal combines with a non-metal. You can usually recognise
ionic compounds because they contain a metal — magnesium oxide, calcium
fluoride and zinc bromide all follow the metal-plus-non-metal pattern. The
book's own hint (below) flags the ammonium exceptions early so the rule
never gets over-learned.

Here is the formation story for NaCl, one step at a time. A sodium atom has
electronic configuration [2, 8, 1] — one outer electron. A chlorine atom has
[2, 8, 7] — room for exactly one more. Chlorine attracts electrons more
strongly than sodium does, so **one electron is transferred** from the sodium's
outer shell to the chlorine's outer shell. Losing an electron leaves sodium
with one more proton than electron: charge 1+. Gaining one leaves chlorine
with one more electron than proton: charge 1−.

:::key-point
Two of the book's KEY POINTs anchor the mechanism. (1) The formation reaction
is a simplification — in reality you don't react sodium *atoms* with chlorine
*atoms* but with chlorine molecules, Cl₂ (chunk 0305); the atom-level story is
the model, not the laboratory recipe. (2) You can check the 1+ charge from the
Periodic Table: sodium has atomic number 11, so 11 protons give an 11+ nucleus;
the atom's 11 electrons cancel it to neutral, but the ion has only 10 electrons
— 11+ against 10− leaves an overall **1+** (chunk 0306).
:::

The charged particles formed are called **[[ion]]s** — charged particles made
when atoms (or groups of atoms) lose or gain electrons. A positive ion is a
**[[cation]]** (for example Na⁺); a negative ion is an **[[anion]]** (for
example Cl⁻). When an ionic compound forms, electrons are transferred from a
metal atom to a non-metal atom, and the compound is held together by strong
**[[electrostatic-attraction]]** — the attraction between the positive and
negative ions just formed (spec 1.41's whole idea in one line).

:::key-point
The book's definitions of record (chunks 0307 + 0308): *electrostatic
attraction simply means that positively charged particles attract negatively
charged particles*; and ionic bonding is often shown using **dot-and-cross
diagrams**, where the transferred electrons are drawn as dots for one atom and
crosses for the other. There is absolutely no difference between the electrons
in reality — dots and crosses only show which atom each electron came from
(two colours of dots, or two colours of crosses, would serve equally well).
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's hint (chunk 0304) protects you from the classic over-generalisation:
*there are one or two exceptions — ionic compounds that do not contain a
metal, for example those containing the ammonium ion (such as NH₄Cl,
(NH₄)₂SO₄)*. So "contains a metal" is a good recognition rule but never a
definition. In "state whether the bonding in X is ionic" questions, ammonium
salts are ionic despite having no metal — the examiners have used this exact
trap.
:::

:::misconception
"Chlorine turns negative because it gains a proton." Protons never move in
chemistry — they are the fixed identity of the nucleus. Gain or loss of
**electrons** is the only charge-changing move: Cl has 17 protons and 17
electrons; Cl⁻ has 17 protons and 18 electrons. The same discipline explains
the sodium side: Na⁺ is still sodium (11 protons) — it has simply lost one of
its 11 electrons.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.37 items — describing ion
formation by electron loss or gain for a named metal/non-metal pair, and
explaining the charge on a named ion from its proton and electron counts.
Spec 1.41 items — stating that ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction
between oppositely charged ions. The book's Figure 7.2 (dot-and-cross for
NaCl) is described in the text; redraw it yourself from the configurations.
:::

sections.title: Ionic bonding in magnesium oxide
sections.markdown:
Magnesium oxide (MgO) is the second worked example, and it adds two new ideas
at once: a **2+/2−** ion pair, and the charge labels that make a
**[[dot-and-cross-diagram]]** complete. Magnesium ([2, 8, 2]) has two outer
electrons; oxygen ([2, 6]) has room for exactly two. **Two electrons are
transferred** from a magnesium atom to an oxygen atom, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.

The book's Figure 7.4 draws the diagram: magnesium's two outer electrons
become crosses inside oxygen's outer shell (or dots-and-crosses in any
colour convention you like — the marks scheme cares about the electron
*count* and the *charges*, not the symbol you used). The caption carries the
single most common lost mark: **don't forget the charges on the ions** — a
correct diagram labelled without Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ is an incomplete answer.

:::key-point
The book's word of the day (chunk 0310, doubled sentence deduplicated):
**isoelectronic** means *have the same number of electrons*. When sodium
forms its ion, electronic configuration [2, 8], it becomes isoelectronic
with neon, [2, 8]. The same idea runs through this whole chapter: Mg²⁺ is
isoelectronic with neon, and O²⁻ is isoelectronic with neon too — three
different particles, one electron count.
:::

Notice what the transfer did *not* do: it did not make a molecule. One Mg²⁺
paired with one O²⁻ is the *formula unit* the diagram shows — the actual
compound (section 12) is a giant lattice of very many Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. The
diagram is the bookkeeping for one transfer; the compound is the sum of
enormous numbers of those transfers' results.

:::exam-hint
Dot-and-cross mark schemes for 1.40 are nearly always the same three lines:
outer shells only (spec words: *only outer electrons need be shown*);
correct electron counts in each ion's outer shell; **charges on both ions**.
For MgO: magnesium bracket [2, 8]²⁺ with empty outer shell, oxygen bracket
[2, 8]²⁻ with eight outer electrons — two of them crosses. Draw big, clear
square brackets; tiny cramped brackets are where marks go missing.
:::

:::misconception
"Mg²⁺ means the magnesium atom gained two electrons, and O²⁻ lost two." Read
the charges against the process: losing electrons leaves *more* protons than
electrons, so **loss makes positive** (Mg lost 2 → 2+); gaining electrons
makes the balance negative (O gained 2 → 2−). The superscript records the
balance after the transfer — never the direction of the move itself.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.40 items — drawing the MgO
dot-and-cross diagram (outer electrons only, charges shown); spec 1.41 items —
identifying the electrostatic attraction between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ as the ionic
bond. Self-check before moving on: can you say *why* the charges are 2+ and
2− from the group numbers alone (Group 2 → 2+; Group 6 → 2−)?
:::

sections.title: Noble gas electronic configurations — and the ions that break the pattern
sections.markdown:
Look back at the ions formed so far — Na⁺, Cl⁻, Mg²⁺, O²⁻ — and a pattern
emerges: every one of them has a **noble gas electronic configuration**,
[2, 8] (neon) or [2, 8, 8] (argon). That is the deep "why" behind ion
formation for the first 20 elements: atoms lose or gain electrons so that
they **achieve a noble gas electronic configuration** — the already-stable
arrangement of Group 0.

The group law follows. Elements in **Groups 1, 2 and 3** *lose* their outer
shell electrons to form **1+, 2+ and 3+** ions; elements in **Groups 5, 6 and
7** *gain* electrons to form **3−, 2− and 1−** ions. The book's worked
corners: aluminium ([2, 8, 3]) loses three electrons → Al³⁺; nitrogen ([2, 5])
gains three → the nitride ion N³⁻. And elements in Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
**always** form ions [[isoelectronic]] with the nearest noble gas: rubidium
(Group 1) loses its one outer electron to become isoelectronic with krypton;
iodine (Group 7) gains one electron to become isoelectronic with xenon.

:::key-point
Spec 1.38's charge table in one view (chunk 0311 + the chapter's Table 7.1,
rendered in section 6): Groups 1/2/3 lose 1/2/3 electrons → 1+/2+/3+;
Groups 5/6/7 gain 3/2/1 → 3−/2−/1−. The group number is the outer-electron
count; the charge is the cheapest route to a full outer shell.
:::

Then the book lands the caveat that keeps 1.38 honest: **a lot of common ions
do not have noble gas structures**. Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺, Ag⁺ and Pb²⁺ are
all ions you will meet across the International GCSE course, and *not one of
them has a noble gas structure* (the book shows the Fe²⁺ ion with the caption
"definitely not a noble gas structure!"). You are not required to write their
electronic configurations — only their charges, learned as data (section 6,
Table 7.2).

:::exam-hint
"Noble gas configuration" is a *description*, not a *cause* you must argue at
this level: for the first 20 elements the stable arrangement explains the
group law, and that is the full depth the spec wants. The exam trap is
over-applying it — a question that offers Fe³⁺ or Zn²⁺ is testing whether you
know the named-ion charges (1.38) rather than the group rule. Learn both
lists and never mix them: group charges for Groups 1/2/3/5/6/7, learned
charges for the six named metals plus H⁺ and the four complex ions.
:::

:::misconception
"Every ion must be isoelectronic with a noble gas — so Fe³⁺ can't exist." It
exists, it's common, and it is not isoelectronic with anything noble — that is
exactly why the book flags it. The noble-gas rule is a *trend for the first 20
elements*, not a law of the universe. Transition-metal and heavy-metal ions
(Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Pb) have their own charges that are learned, not derived.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.37 items — predicting whether
an element loses or gains electrons, and how many, from its position; spec
1.38 items — stating the charges of Group 1/2/3 metals and Group 5/6/7
non-metals, and recalling the named-ion list. The book's own extensions
(Rb→Kr, I→Xe) make good self-test material: cover the text and derive each
result.
:::

sections.title: Other examples of ionic bonding — lithium fluoride and calcium chloride
sections.markdown:
The book's "other examples" section pairs a 1+/1− case with a 2+/1− case, so
you see the *same* transfer logic producing different formulas. Printed
heading provenance: the book pages this under "CALCIUM CHLORIDE", but the
chunk (and the printed page) actually runs lithium fluoride first (Figure
7.9), then calcium chloride (Figure 7.10) — both are carried here in book
order.

**Lithium fluoride, LiF.** The lithium atom has 1 outer electron that is
easily lost; fluorine has space to receive exactly one. One electron is
transferred from lithium to fluorine, giving Li⁺ and F⁻. Lithium fluoride is
held together by the strong [[electrostatic-attraction]] between positive
Li⁺ ions and negative F⁻ ions. One of each — the simplest possible ratio.

**Calcium chloride, CaCl₂.** The calcium atom [2, 8, 8, 2] has **two**
outer electrons, but each chlorine atom [2, 8, 7] has room to take only
**one**. You therefore need **two chlorines for every calcium**: the two
electrons are transferred from one calcium atom to two separate chlorine
atoms, one each. The formula is CaCl₂ — and because the Ca²⁺ ion is doubly
charged, the electrostatic attractions holding the ions together are very
strong.

:::key-point
The general law hiding in these two examples (chunk 0314): the *ratio* in
the formula is set by how many electrons must move and how many each
partner can accept or lose. Li gives 1, F takes 1 → LiF. Ca gives 2, Cl
takes 1 each → two Cl per Ca → CaCl₂. Section 6 turns this counting law
into the general formula shortcut.
:::

Note also what the diagrams do *not* show: CaCl₂'s diagram (Figure 7.10)
draws one calcium and two chlorines because that is the *ratio*, not
because a CaCl₂ unit floats around as a thing. Like every ionic compound,
calcium chloride is a giant lattice (section 12) — the dot-and-cross
diagram is the accounting for one calcium's two electrons.

:::exam-hint
For a "draw the dot-and-cross diagram for calcium chloride" question (1.40),
the mark scheme wants: calcium with empty outer shell labelled 2+, **two**
chlorine outer shells each labelled 1− and each showing eight outer
electrons (one of them a cross from calcium). The classic error is drawing
one chlorine receiving two electrons — a chlorine outer shell holds only
eight, and the 1− charge says it took one. Two transfer arrows to two
separate ions is the correct picture.
:::

:::misconception
"Calcium shares its two electrons, one with each chlorine." Sharing is
*covalent* bonding (Chapter 8); here the electrons **transfer** and stay —
each chlorine walks away with both of its new electrons permanently, and
the calcium is left 2+. The tell is in the products: charged ions (Ca²⁺,
2 Cl⁻), which is why the compound conducts when molten and needs the
electrostatic-lattice description of the sections that follow.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.40 items — dot-and-cross
diagrams for LiF and CaCl₂ (Groups 1/2 × Group 7, outer electrons only);
spec 1.41 items — identifying the electrostatic attraction between the
named ions as the bond. If you can draw CaCl₂ correctly, every Group-2 ×
Group-7 combination in past papers is the same skill with different
symbols.
:::

sections.title: Formulae for ionic compounds
sections.markdown:
There are far too many ionic compounds on the course to learn formulae one
by one — the book is blunt about it: *you need a simple, shortcut method*.
The method rests on one non-negotiable law.

**The law: equal numbers of pluses and minuses.** Ions are formed when atoms
or groups of atoms lose or gain electrons, and every compound is electrically
**neutral** — so an ionic compound must contain the right number of each ion
for the total positive charge to cancel the total negative charge exactly.
To apply it you need the charges, and there are two ways to get them.

**Where you can work the charge out.** The group law from section 4, in the
book's own Table 7.1 (chunk 0322):

| Group in the Periodic Table | Charge on ion | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1+ | Na⁺ |
| 2 | 2+ | Mg²⁺ |
| 3 | 3+ | Al³⁺ |
| 5 | 3− | N³⁻ |
| 6 | 2− | O²⁻ |
| 7 | 1− | Br⁻ |

:::key-point
Chunk 0323 adds the two reading rules for Table 7.1. Any element in Group 2
has 2 outer electrons and loses them all → 2+; any element in Group 6 has 6
outer electrons and room for 2 more → 2−; similar arguments fix the other
groups shown. And the REMINDER (chunk 0319) stands behind every row: **all
metals form positive ions.**
:::

**Where the name tells you the charge.** For metals that form more than one
ion, the name carries the charge in Roman numerals: lead(II) oxide contains
Pb²⁺; iron(III) chloride contains Fe³⁺; copper(II) sulfate contains Cu²⁺.
The number in brackets *is* the number of charges.

:::key-point
Chunk 0321 gives the metal-free exception its full picture: ammonium
chloride (NH₄Cl) is ionic — there is ionic bonding between the NH₄⁺ and
Cl⁻ ions — yet *inside* the NH₄⁺ ion the N–H links are covalent (Chapter
8). An ionic compound can therefore contain covalent bonds in its
polyatomic ion; the two descriptions apply at different scales.
:::

**The learn-list.** Some charges cannot be worked out at all — the book's
Table 7.2 (chunk 0324), verbatim (OCR repairs disclosed in the receipt):

| Charge | Substance | Ion |
|---|---|---|
| positive | zinc | Zn²⁺ |
|  | silver | Ag⁺ |
|  | hydrogen | H⁺ |
|  | ammonium | NH₄⁺ |
| negative | nitrate | NO₃⁻ |
|  | hydroxide | OH⁻ |
|  | carbonate | CO₃²⁻ |
|  | sulfate | SO₄²⁻ |

:::key-point
Chunks 0326 + 0328 close the method. (1) These learn-list ions are the
difficult ones — learn **both the formula and the charge** for each; you
will meet others later, but this eight is the working set. (2) The brackets
law: when a formula needs **more than one** of a multi-atom
complex ion, write brackets — barium nitrate is
Ba(NO₃)₂; without the brackets, "BaNO32" would read as 1 barium, 1
nitrogen and **32 oxygens**. Anywhere else, brackets are unnecessary.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's hint (chunk 0318) removes the last excuse: *you will always have
a copy of the Periodic Table, even in an exam*, so the group charges are
always available. What the table cannot tell you: lead forms Pb²⁺ (Group 4
elements form few ionic compounds and the situation is more complicated) —
Pb²⁺ rides on the named-ion list. Exam routine: group charges from the
Periodic Table; named charges from memory; Roman numerals from the name.
:::

:::misconception
"Ionic formulae are 100% memorisation." Only the eight learn-list charges
are memory; everything else is *derivation*. Balance the charges and count:
a 2+ ion meeting a 1− ion needs two of the 1− ion; a 3+ meeting a 2− needs
three and two respectively (6+ balances 6−). Learners who memorise formulae
one at a time drown by Unit 2; learners who balance charges write unfamiliar
formulae — aluminium sulfate, sodium carbonate — on demand.
:::

:::maths-skills
Balancing ion charges is a **common-multiple** problem wearing a chemistry
coat. Fe³⁺ brings 3 units; SO₄²⁻ brings 2 — the smallest total both can
reach is the lowest common multiple, 6, which takes 2 irons and 3 sulfates.
The same arithmetic the book's crossover exploits (Figure 7.13): swapping
the two charge numbers *is* dividing by the product over each charge.
Whenever the charge pair shares a factor (2+/2−, 3+/3−, 2+/4− beyond this
course), the LCM view also tells you the ratio will simplify — CaO not
Ca₂O₂.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.38 items — charges of the
learn-list ions and group charges; spec 1.39 items — formulae from ion
pairs (both-sides drilling: Na⁺/O²⁻; Ca²⁺/Cl⁻; NH₄⁺/SO₄²⁻). The section's
two tables are the recall targets; the word-endings warning the book
attaches here (chunk 0327) gets its own section next.
:::

sections.title: Confusing endings — -ide and -ate
sections.markdown:
Two name-endings decide what a compound contains, and mixing them up is one
of the most common formula errors on the course (the book says so — the hint
is quoted in section 6's census and repeated here because this page is where
it pays).

**-ide: nothing complicated.** An *-ide* name means the compound contains
exactly the elements named and nothing else. Sodium chloride is just sodium
and chlorine combined; copper(II) **sulfide** contains copper and sulfur
only — Cu²⁺ and S²⁻ ions, formula **CuS** (the book's Figure 7.11).

**-ate: oxygen is there too.** An *-ate* name means oxygen (and possibly
other things) is present as well. Copper(II) **sulfate** contains copper,
sulfur **and oxygen** — Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻, formula **CuSO₄** (Figure 7.12).

:::exam-hint
The book's warning (chunk 0327): *not looking carefully at word endings is
one of the most common mistakes students make when they start to write
formulae.* Exam drill: read the ending FIRST — -ide → two-element pair;
-ate → oxygen present — then pick the ion from the learn-list. Sulfide S²⁻
versus sulfate SO₄²⁻; nitride N³⁻ versus nitrate NO₃⁻; chloride Cl⁻ versus
chlorate (you will not need chlorate on this course, but the ending logic
already tells you it carries oxygen).
:::

:::misconception
"-ate just sounds more chemical — the ending doesn't carry information." The
ending is a compressed composition statement, and it changes the ion you
select: copper(II) sulfide and copper(II) sulfate differ by a whole ion
(S²⁻ versus SO₄²⁻) and therefore by a whole formula (CuS versus CuSO₄).
Misreading one letter flips the answer — which is exactly why examiners
like the pair.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.39 items — selecting the
correct ion from an -ide/-ate name before writing the formula (CuS vs
CuSO₄; NaCl vs Na₂SO₄-style pairs). Quick self-test: name the ions in
magnesium sulfide, magnesium sulfate, calcium nitride and calcium nitrate —
then write all four formulae by balancing charges.
:::

sections.title: To find the formula for sodium oxide
sections.markdown:
The book now runs the method on worked examples, and the first one is
deliberately the smallest case where a plain "1:1 cancels" reflex fails.

**Sodium oxide.** Sodium is in Group 1, so the ion is Na⁺. Oxygen is in
Group 6, so the ion is O²⁻. To equalise the charges you need **two sodium
ions** (2 × 1+ = 2+) for **one oxide ion** (2−): the 2+ from two sodiums
cancels the 2− of one oxide. The formula is therefore **Na₂O**.

(A provenance note, disclosed in the receipt: the parse of record prints
"The formula is therefore NaO" — the chunker's OCR dropped the subscript 2.
The chunk's own reasoning sentence — *two sodium ions to provide the two
positive charges* — pins the correct Na₂O, and every downstream use in the
book confirms it. The prose carries the repaired formula with this
disclosure; the printed-heading text itself is retained as provenance.)

The worked example is short because the method is short: name the ions,
count the charges, scale to balance, write the formula with the counts as
subscripts. Forty seconds in an exam, one mark banked.

:::exam-hint
Write the ion charges ABOVE the symbols before scaling: Na⁺ over Na, O²⁻
over O. The intermediate "2 Na⁺ per 1 O²⁻" line is what the mark scheme's
"balancing charges" credit rewards — and it catches the slide back to "NaO"
because the 2− makes you look for *two* positives, not one. Subscripts
belong to the atom that needs multiplying: Na₂O, never NaO₂ (two oxygens
would give 4− against 2+).
:::

:::misconception
"Na⁺ and O²⁻ — the + and − cancel 1-for-1, so NaO." The cancellation is
between total charge *magnitudes*, not between ions. One Na⁺ carries one
unit of positive charge; one O²⁻ carries TWO units of negative. Neutral
happens at two positives per one negative — 2+ against 2−. The charge
*number* (the superscript) is how many units each ion brings; the formula
counts how many ions bring it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.38 items — recalling Na⁺
(Group 1) and O²⁻ (Group 6); spec 1.39 items — writing Na₂O from the
balanced-charge argument. Extension joins from the same skill: K₂O, Li₂O,
and the reverse-reading question "why is sodium peroxide Na₂O₂ not on this
course's list?" (its ion is not the plain oxide — beyond the spec, but a
good check that the endings law from section 7 stays in scope).
:::

sections.title: To find the formula for barium nitrate
sections.markdown:
The second worked example adds the one piece of syntax the method needs:
**brackets around a multi-atom ion** when more than one of it appears.

**Barium nitrate.** Barium is in Group 2, so the ion is Ba²⁺. Nitrate ions
are NO₃⁻ — a [[complex-ion]] (an ion made of more than one atom) whose
charge you *remember*, not derive (Table 7.2, section 6). To equalise
charges you need **two nitrate ions for each barium ion** (2+ against
2 × 1−). The formula is **Ba(NO₃)₂**.

The brackets are load-bearing, not decoration: they say "everything inside
is doubled". Written without them the formula reads BaNO₃₂ — and the book's
KEY POINT makes the absurdity vivid: *that would read as 1 barium, 1
nitrogen and 32 oxygens!* With brackets: 1 barium, 2 nitrogens, 6 oxygens.

:::key-point
Chunk 0333 answers a question learners are often shy to ask — why don't
formulae show the charges? They *can*: sodium chloride is sometimes written
Na⁺Cl⁻ to make a point about the ions present. But for most purposes the
charges are left out: **in an ionic compound the charges are there, whether
you write them or not.** The formula records the neutral ratio; the charge
labels live on the ions, and on dot-and-cross diagrams.
:::

:::exam-hint
Brackets law in one line: brackets appear **only** when a complex ion is
multiplied. Ba(NO₃)₂ yes; Na₂SO₄ yes (sulfate doubled); NaNO₃ no (one
nitrate — brackets would be harmless but non-standard); NaCl no. When a
mark scheme says "correct use of brackets", it is checking exactly this
rule — and the (NO₃)₂ must be followed by the subscript *outside* the
bracket, never inside.
:::

:::misconception
"Ba(NO₃)₂ and BaNO₃₂ are the same formula written differently." They name
different substances: the bracketed form is 1 Ba, 2 N, 6 O; the unbracketed
run-together reads 1 Ba, 1 N, 32 O — physically nothing. The 2 in a formula
always multiplies *what it follows*: following a bracket it doubles the
whole ion; following an element symbol it multiplies only that element. That
subtle reading is why the bracket exists.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.38 items — recalling NO₃⁻
and Ba²⁺; spec 1.39 items — writing bracketed formulae for Group-2 ×
nitrate/hydroxide/carbonate pairs (Ba(NO₃)₂, Ca(OH)₂, Na₂CO₃, K₂SO₄). The
oxygen-count check (6 oxygens in Ba(NO₃)₂) is a fast self-audit the
examiners also use in "explain why the formula is wrong" items.
:::

sections.title: To find the formula for iron(III) sulfate
sections.markdown:
The third worked example is the hard case the method was built for: a 3+
metal against a 2− complex ion. (Provenance: the section map's printed
heading carries the OCR misread of iron(III) — the capital-I/lowercase-L
corruption class flagged in finding f-0010 — repaired to iron(III)
throughout, disclosed in the receipt.)

**Iron(III) sulfate.** Iron(III) tells you the metal ion is Fe³⁺ (the name
carries the charge — section 6's Roman-numeral rule). Sulfate ions are
SO₄²⁻. Balancing: you need **two iron(III) ions for every three sulfate
ions** — 2 × 3+ = 6+ and 3 × 2− = 6−, equal and opposite. The formula is
**Fe₂(SO₄)₃**.

Both syntax laws fire at once: the subscript 2 on iron (multiplied because
2 ions are needed) and the brackets with subscript 3 on sulfate (a complex
ion multiplied). Total audit: 2 Fe, 4 × 3 = 12 O, charges 6+ = 6−.

:::key-point
The book's shortcut (Figure 7.13, chunk 0334): to work out complicated
formulae, **cross over the numbers in the charges** — the 3 from Fe³⁺
becomes the sulfate count; the 2 from SO₄²⁻ becomes the iron count.
Fe³⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Fe₂(SO₄)₃ in one move. The crossover *is* the balanced-
charge arithmetic in disguise; the totals check (6+/6−) is always available
to prove it.
:::

:::exam-hint
The crossover shortcut is fast but it is *presentational* — the marks sit in
the balancing statement. Write "6+ and 6−" (or "2 × 3+ balances 3 × 2−")
before the formula: that sentence earns the marks even if the final formula
slips, and it catches the classic slip of crossing over to Fe₃(SO₄)₂ (which
gives 9+/4− — instantly unbalanced). In "explain why Fe₂(SO₄)₃ is the
correct formula" items, the totals line IS the answer.
:::

:::misconception
"3+ and 2− balance each other directly, so the formula is FeSO₄ with the
charges noted." FeSO₄ is iron(II) sulfate — a *different salt* made of
Fe²⁺. Charges balance as totals across the whole formula unit, not
ion-by-ion: 3+ against 2− needs the lowest common multiple (6), which takes
2 irons and 3 sulfates. The Roman numeral in the name is the charge of the
metal ion — and iron(II) versus iron(III) formulas are the standard exam
pair for testing exactly this.
:::

:::maths-skills
The crossover (Figure 7.13) is a **digit-swap** shortcut with a built-in
audit. Swap the magnitudes — 3 lands on the sulfate count, 2 on the iron
count — then verify by totals: 2 × 3+ = 6+ and 3 × 2− = 6−. The audit is
the safety net the swap lacks: applied blindly to Ca²⁺ + O²⁻ it yields
Ca₂O₂, and the totals check (4+ = 4−) says "consistent but not lowest" —
simplify to CaO. Swap, then always re-add the charges; if the sums are not
equal, the formula is wrong, whatever the swap said.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.38 items — Fe³⁺ from the
name iron(III), SO₄²⁻ from the learn-list; spec 1.39 items — writing
Fe₂(SO₄)₃ and siblings (Al₂(SO₄)₃, FePO₄-style 3+/3− pairs, CuCO₃ vs
CuSO₄). Drill the totals check: every formula you write, verify the charge
sums to zero before moving on.
:::

sections.title: Calcium chloride provides another example
sections.markdown:
The book closes the formulae block by running the crossover method back
onto calcium chloride — and by showing where the shortcut must NOT be
trusted.

**CaCl₂ by crossover (Figure 7.14).** Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻: cross the 2 to the
chlorine and… nothing to the calcium, because *there is no extra number in
front of the charge on Cl⁻ — we do not tend to write in a 1*. The charge
"1−" carries an unwritten 1, so the crossover gives Ca₁Cl₂, written simply
**CaCl₂**.

**The trap: same charges (Figure 7.15).** Try the crossover on calcium
oxide and it hands you Ca₂O₂ — 2+ crossed to oxygen, 2− crossed to calcium.
The book's correction: *the formula of calcium oxide is CaO and not Ca₂O₂*.
When the charges on the two ions are the same, there is already 1 of each
in the neutral ratio — nothing needs swapping, and the formula is the plain
pair: **CaO**, MgO, NaCl, LiF. (Ca₂O₂ isn't *wrong* as an arithmetic fact —
2+ per 2− — it is simply never written: formulae use the lowest whole-number
ratio.)

:::exam-hint
Crossover protocol for exams: (1) write both charges; (2) if the two charge
*magnitudes* are equal, stop — the formula is one of each (CaO, BaO, NaF);
(3) otherwise cross over and simplify nothing (the crossed numbers are
already the lowest pair for the exam's compounds); (4) brackets only around
multi-atom ions (Fe₂(SO₄)₃, not Fe₂SO₄₃). The Ca₂O₂ trap is a real
"spot-the-error" item format — now you know both halves of the answer: the
ratio 1:1, and why.
:::

:::misconception
"Ca₂O₂ simplifies to CaO, so writing Ca₂O₂ shows the ions better and should
score." Formulae of ionic compounds are written in their **lowest
whole-number ratio** — that is the convention every mark scheme applies,
because the compound is a giant lattice with no discrete Ca₂O₂ unit to
point at. The ion charges are shown on diagrams and in explanations, not
inside the compound's formula.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.39 items — formulae
from ion pairs where charges are equal vs unequal: CaO vs CaCl₂; MgO vs
MgCl₂; BaO vs Ba(NO₃)₂). Self-test: write the six formulae for the pairs
{Mg²⁺, Ba²⁺} × {O²⁻, Cl⁻, OH⁻} — three need brackets, three don't.
:::

sections.title: Giant ionic structures
sections.markdown:
Everything so far described the *bookkeeping* of electron transfer. This
section zooms out to the actual substance: what a crystal of sodium
chloride physically is.

**All ionic compounds form crystals** consisting of **lattices** of
positive and negative ions packed together in a regular way. A
**[[lattice]]** is a regular array of particles — the book's everyday
analogy (Figure 7.16) is literally a lattice fence: a repeating pattern
that extends as far as you care to look. The ionic lattice is held together
by the strong [[electrostatic-attraction]] between the positively and
negatively charged ions, and in a **[[giant-ionic-lattice]]** that
attraction runs throughout the whole structure, in all directions.

:::exam-hint
The book prints this hint in bold urgency (chunk 0338): *you must not talk
about molecules of an ionic compound — this will be marked wrong in the
exam and you could lose all the marks for a question!* Say instead: ions,
lattice, giant structure, formula unit. The habit matters in every later
answer — "NaCl molecules exist in solution", "one molecule of MgO" — all
zero-mark phrasings. In electrolysis and structure questions (Units 1 and
2), the words "ions free to move" only make sense once "no molecules" is
reflex.
:::

:::misconception
"A crystal of NaCl is a huge molecule made of lots of NaCl units stuck
together." There are no NaCl units to stick together — that is precisely
what "giant" rules out. The structure is one continuous array of Na⁺ and
Cl⁻ ions with no natural boundary or repeat unit you could lift out and
call a molecule; any fragment you pick is arbitrary. The chemical formula
NaCl records the 1:1 *ratio*, not a particle that exists on its own.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The lattice is mathematics made solid: a **regular repeating array** is
exactly what a tessellation or wallpaper pattern is in geometry — one unit
cell (here, the 6-around-6 sodium-chloride arrangement) translated again and
again to fill space with no gaps. Crystallography, the science built on that
idea, won Nobel prizes by applying X-ray diffraction to precisely the
lattices this chapter describes — the same repeating-array mathematics also
underlies wallpaper groups, tiling problems and the way metals are forged.
When the book reaches for a lattice fence (Figure 7.16) to explain the word,
it is pointing at one of chemistry's deepest exports to mathematics.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.42 items — describing the
giant ionic lattice (regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions, held
by electrostatic attraction) and explaining why the word "molecule" never
applies. This description is the setup for the melting-point argument in
section 14 — the two are nearly always examined together.
:::

sections.title: The structure of magnesium oxide
sections.markdown:
The book takes one crystal and dissects it. In diagrams the ions of sodium
chloride are usually drawn in an **"exploded" view** (Figure 7.18): each
sodium ion is surrounded by **6 chloride ions**, and each chloride ion is
surrounded by **6 sodium ions** — and that 6-around-6 pattern repeats
throughout the structure over vast numbers of ions. The lines in the
exploded diagram are not bonds; they only show which ions touch.

This is the **[[giant-ionic-lattice]]** in its full sense: *giant* is not
"big" — it means a structure with **no individual molecules**. All the
sodium ions attract all the chloride ions; you cannot pick out a sodium
chloride molecule, because none exists. The bonding extends throughout the
structure in every direction, with no limit to the particle count — all we
know is that the numbers of sodium and chloride ions must be equal.

**Magnesium oxide has exactly the same structure** — Mg²⁺ in place of Na⁺,
O²⁻ in place of Cl⁻, the same 6-around-6 lattice. The difference is force:
the magnesium oxide lattice is held together by **stronger
[[electrostatic-attraction]]**, because 2+ ions are attracting 2− ions,
where sodium chloride's attractions run only between 1+ and 1− ions.
(Extension work from the book: Mg²⁺ is also smaller than Na⁺ and O²⁻
smaller than Cl⁻, which raises the attraction further — but the charge
effect is the more important one.)

:::key-point
The 6-around-6 number and the "no molecules" law are the two facts examiners
probe in structure questions: describe the coordination (each ion surrounded
by six of the opposite charge) and name the force (electrostatic attraction
between oppositely charged ions, extending throughout the giant lattice).
The same-structure-different-strength comparison of MgO vs NaCl is the
classic "explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium
chloride" answer at this level: higher charges → stronger attraction → more
energy to break the lattice.
:::

:::exam-hint
When explaining melting-point differences (spec 1.42), anchor every step to
the lattice: charge → attraction strength → energy to separate → melting
point. "MgO has stronger ionic bonds because the ions are charged 2+/2−"
scores; "MgO's bonds are just stronger" scores nothing — the examiner wants
the *property of the ions* (charge) linked to the *property of the lattice*
(attraction) to the *observable* (melting point). Keep the exploded-view
detail in reserve for "describe the structure" items: 6 of each, repeating,
no molecules.
:::

:::misconception
"The lines in the exploded lattice diagram are the ionic bonds — six bonds
per sodium ion." The book pre-empts this: the lines are *not* bonds, they
show touching/arrangement. Each ion's attraction is not six private links
but an electrostatic pull on all nearby oppositely charged ions, extending
throughout the giant lattice. Drawing conventions ≠ physical bonds — the
same discipline as dot-and-cross dots (section 2): notation is bookkeeping,
the physics is the attraction.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.41 items — naming the force
holding the lattice (electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged
ions); spec 1.42 items — explaining MgO's higher melting point against
NaCl via the 2+/2− versus 1+/1− charge comparison. Sketch the exploded
NaCl/MgO lattice from memory with the 6-around-6 counts labelled.
:::

sections.title: The physical properties of ionic substances
sections.markdown:
Four properties, one cause. (Provenance note: the book prints the brittleness
and solubility sentences on the chapter-questions page, and the chunker swept
them into the questions chunk 0345 ahead of the printed question list — they
are section prose here, with the questions staying page-jump-only, exactly the
c06 Example-4 spillover precedent.)

**High melting and boiling points.** Ionic compounds have high melting points
and boiling points **because of the strong electrostatic forces of attraction
holding the lattice together**: a lot of energy must be supplied to break the
attractions between the many oppositely charged ions in the giant structure.
(spec 1.42's whole demand.)

**Crystalline.** Ionic compounds tend to be crystalline — the visible echo of
the regular lattice. Some crystals are too small to see: magnesium oxide is
always a white powder because its individual crystals are microscopic.

**Brittle.** Ionic crystals tend to be brittle: any small distortion of the
crystal brings ions of the **same charge** alongside each other — like
charges repel — and the crystal splits itself apart along that plane (the
book's Figure 7.20 diagrams the repulsion between same-charge ions doing the
splitting).

**Solubility pattern.** Ionic substances tend to be **soluble in water** and
**insoluble in organic solvents** (ethanol, hexane and the petrol hydrocarbons
are the book's examples — chunk 0343). Extension work (chunk 0346): water is
*polar* — its shared electrons sit nearer the oxygen, leaving oxygen slightly
negative and the hydrogens slightly positive — so water molecules form strong
enough attractions to ions to pull the lattice apart. Hexane is non-polar and
cannot. Not every ionic salt obeys: magnesium oxide is insoluble in water —
its 2+/2− attractions are too strong for the water molecules to overcome.

:::key-point
Chunk 0343's vocabulary note: **organic solvents** include ethanol (alcohol)
and hydrocarbons such as hexane and the mixture in petrol — the Unit-4
organic chemistry of this course names the family. The property pair to
recall: soluble in water; insoluble in organic solvents.
:::

:::exam-hint
The book's hint (chunk 0344): *molten just means the salt has been melted —
it is a liquid.* The word appears in every conductivity and electrolysis
question: "molten sodium chloride" = melted NaCl, ions free to move;
"aqueous" = dissolved in water, same conclusion. Both words are route words,
not chemistry content — know them cold so a vocabulary wobble never costs a
physics-of-ions mark. (Spec 1.42's melting-point explanation gets its marks
from the lattice-energy chain of section 13, not from the word "strong".)
:::

:::misconception
"Ionic compounds have high melting points because an ionic bond is stronger
than a covalent bond." The comparison is not bond-versus-bond — it is
structure-versus-structure. Melting means separating the particles of the
lattice, and in a giant lattice *every* ion is attracting *many* oppositely
charged neighbours: you must overcome a vast network of attractions, not one
pair. State it structurally — strong electrostatic attraction throughout the
giant lattice, much energy to break — and the mark scheme's levels are all
covered.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join (derived-links law): spec 1.42 items — explaining high
melting/boiling points via the giant lattice; predicting property
differences (brittle; water-soluble vs organic-insoluble) from the ionic
structure. Quick audit of the four properties: for each, can you name the
lattice feature that causes it without looking back?
:::

sections.title: The electrical conductivity of ionic substances — and the chapter close
sections.markdown:
The last spec point is a two-state rule with one forbidden word.

**When solid:** ionic compounds **do not conduct** electricity — the ions are
**fixed in position** in the lattice and are not free to move around. **When
[[molten]]** (melted) **or in [[aqueous-solution]]** (dissolved in water):
they **do conduct** — because the ions then become **free to move** and can
carry the charge through the liquid.

The book underlines the language with its own warning: *it is really
important that you use the correct words when explaining this. Do not use
the word "electrons". You must talk about the ions being free to move.* The
charge carriers in an ionic conductor are **ions** — that single substitution
is the whole answer.

:::summary
In one page: **formation** — metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them;
the charged particles are ions (cation +, anion −). **Diagrams** —
dot-and-cross, outer shells only, charges labelled. **Charges** — Groups
1/2/3 lose 1/2/3 electrons (1+/2+/3+); Groups 5/6/7 gain 3/2/1 (3−/2−/1−);
plus the learned list Zn²⁺, Ag⁺, H⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, OH⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻ (not all
ions are noble-gas configurations — Fe³⁺ and friends). **Formulae** — equal
pluses and minuses; brackets only when a complex ion is multiplied;
-ide = two elements, -ate = oxygen present; crossover with the
same-charges trap (CaO, not Ca₂O₂). **Structure** — giant ionic lattice,
no molecules, 6-around-6. **Properties** — high melting/boiling points
(strong electrostatic attraction throughout the lattice), crystalline,
brittle, water-soluble/organic-insoluble, and conducting only when molten
or aqueous because only then are the ions free to move.
:::

:::can-you
- Explain how a sodium atom and a chlorine atom become Na⁺ and Cl⁻, and why the compound is neutral overall? (1.37)
- State the charges of ions for Groups 1, 2, 3 and 5, 6, 7, and recall the eight learn-list ions? (1.38)
- Write formulae on demand — Na₂O, CaCl₂, Ba(NO₃)₂, Fe₂(SO₄)₃, CuSO₄, (NH₄)₂SO₄ — with brackets in the right places? (1.39)
- Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for NaCl, MgO and CaCl₂, outer shells only, charges shown? (1.40)
- Say what ionic bonding is, in one phrase, without naming electrons as the carrier? (1.41)
- Explain high melting points from the giant lattice, and why MgO beats NaCl? (1.42)
- State when ionic compounds conduct and why — using "ions free to move", never "electrons"? (1.43)
:::

:::exam-hint
The chapter's question bank (p. 83) is two multi-part items — electronic
configurations of the ions in three named reactions, then dot-and-cross
diagrams for K/F, Ca/Br and Mg/I (three Group-1/2 × Group-7 combinations
you have now met as families). Those stay page-jump-only (licensing law) —
but note how every part maps onto a section of this Lesson, which is the
shape of nearly every ionic-bonding question in past papers: configurations
→ diagram → formula, in that order.
:::

:::misconception
"Solid ionic compounds don't conduct because their electrons can't move."
Swap the carrier word and the answer is correct: the ions are the charge
carriers, and in the solid they are locked in the lattice. Writing
"electrons" in a 1.43 answer costs the mark even though the sentence sounds
physical — the spec words are *ions fixed in position* (solid) and *ions
free to move* (molten/aqueous). The forbidden word is the tell that the
learner has confused this with metallic conduction (Chapter 9).
:::
